title: Getting better at systems thinking
author: Nick Hart
summary: Having argued that schools are complex adaptive systems, Hart turns to the harder question of how leaders actually get better at thinking that way. His obstacle is developmental: citing Neil Gilbride's research on headteachers, he notes that a leader's capacity to appreciate complexity and ambiguity is bounded by their stage of adult ego development, and that movement through those stages requires disruptive experience. Rather than wait for disruption, he proposes systematising sense-making, on the grounds that school leadership is problem solving and that experts differ from novices in seeing the deeper structure of problems. The result is a five-step routine for how a leadership team talks about a problem: classify it as wicked or tame, move down the iceberg to underlying causes before jumping to solutions, check it against known system archetypes, interrogate the basis of the team's own thinking, and finally test options against Senge's principles for intended and unintended consequences. The archetypes are doing particular work here, supplying candidate patterns for the otherwise wide-open questions of what has been happening and what is causing it. The underlying bet is that a shared conversational routine can substitute for individual developmental stage.
points: The Gilbride point is the uncomfortable one: a leader's ceiling on handling ambiguity is developmental, so exhortation to 'think systemically' will not move a team that has no routine.
Classifying a problem as wicked or tame before discussing solutions is a cheap gate that prevents tame-problem tooling being aimed at wicked problems.
Hart uses system archetypes as prompts rather than labels, arguing they surface patterns a team would not otherwise think to look for.
Step four builds in reflexivity - questioning why we think what we think - so that shared sense-making does not simply launder the team's biases into a decision.
Senge's principles are applied at the options stage specifically to force consideration of unintended consequences before commitment.
quotes: If we accept that schools are complex adaptive systems that require systems thinking in order to lead them, then it follows that an important responsibility of school leaders is to get better at systems thinking. The problem here is that it might not come easily.

Neil Gilbride’s research shows that our (Headteachers) ability to appreciate the complexity and ambiguity of the systems in which we work are limited by our stage of adult ego development (the ego being the place in the psyche where we make sense of the world around us). Put simply, we need to have disruptive experiences in order to move through stages of adult ego development so this post suggest ways that we can systematise our sense making so that we and the leaders around us can get better at systems thinking.

School leadership is problem solving. Experts see the deeper structure of problems rather than just the surface features so creating a routine for how we talk about problems can nudge us into better systems thinking.

Let’s get better at systems thinking by deliberately being more reflexive. We may start arriving at conclusions after some shared sense making but we all have biases. Questioning the basis of our thinking can help us to surface those biases before we commit to any action.

To get better at systems thinking, let’s prompt ourselves to remember the principles of systems thinking before we launch into our solutions. When we get the point of exploring options for decision making, Senge’s systems thinking principles can help us to interrogate possible courses of action and consider the intended and unintended consequences of our options.
